common_name: April Kiss Camellia (Cold-Hardy Deep Rose-Pink Parks Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; part of Dr. Clifford Parks's cold-hardy April series bred at Camellia Forest Nursery.

directions: April Kiss produces small, deep rose-pink formal double flowers, typically the earliest of the April series to open, on a compact, upright, moderately slow-growing shrub with glossy evergreen foliage. It was bred by Dr. Clifford Parks by crossing hardy Camellia japonica selections and is reliably hardy to USDA zone 6b, well beyond the typical zone 7 limit for most japonicas. In Gulf Coast gardens its bloom shifts earlier into the milder Southern winter rather than true April; further north it flowers as named, timed to dodge the worst late-winter freezes. Plant in partial shade with protection from harsh winter wind for the healthiest foliage.

common_name: April Rose Camellia (Cold-Hardy Rose-Red Parks Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other members of the Parks April series, benefits from fall planting so it is well rooted before its first cold winter.

directions: April Rose bears plump buds that open to formal double, rose-pink flowers on a compact, well-formed, relatively slow-growing shrub, blooming in spring, later than April Kiss within the series. It was originated by Dr. Clifford Parks of Chapel Hill, North Carolina as part of the April series of extra-cold-hardy camellias bred for zone 6b gardens. Its compact habit makes it a good choice for foundation plantings and smaller shade borders where a full-size japonica would outgrow the space. Grow in partial shade in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil.

common_name: April Blush Camellia (Cold-Hardy Rose-to-Shell-Pink Parks Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; tolerates USDA zone 6b, so fall planting gives it a full season to establish before a cold winter.

directions: April Blush is a seedling of Berenice Boddy crossed with Dr. Tinsley, producing large, semi-double, rose-to-shell-pink flowers with yellow anthers and cream filaments over a long mid-to-late season. It was bred by Dr. Clifford Parks as part of the April series of camellias selected for extreme cold hardiness, reliably surviving winters as cold as USDA zone 6b. The compact, slow-growing plant carries lustrous dark green foliage and smooth gray bark, and sets buds heavily. Grow in part shade in consistently moist, acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil.

common_name: Navajo Camellia (White Sasanqua with Carmine Picotee Edge)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; blooms in the cooler months, so fall planting establishes roots ahead of its winter-into-spring flowering.

directions: Navajo produces sizable semi-double flowers in white edged with a ribbon of carmine-red along the petal margins, opening from winter into spring in mild Southern climates. It grows as a slow-growing, upright-to-spreading shrub that becomes small-tree-like with age, carrying oval, glossy evergreen leaves typical of sasanquas. Like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica, making it useful where only partial shade is available, and LSU AgCenter recommends sasanquas like Navajo for Gulf Coast landscapes. Plant high, with the trunk base above grade, in acidic, well-drained soil protected from prolonged hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; upright, rapid growth benefits from a full cool season to root in before summer heat.

directions: Fashionata bears large, semi-double flowers of bright apricot-pink with fashionably curled and frilled petals surrounding a central boss of golden stamens, blooming midseason. It arose as a chance seedling found by Fred Everette of Mobile, Alabama, first flowering around 1960 and introduced in 1964. The shrub is upright, open, and notably fast-growing for a camellia japonica, with dark green foliage, and spent flowers drop cleanly rather than browning on the plant. Grow in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, and prune lightly after bloom to encourage a fuller habit.

common_name: Pink Champagne Camellia (Soft Pink Loose Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; a late bloomer, so fall planting gives it a full season of root growth before its late-winter flower show.

directions: Pink Champagne produces large, soft pink flowers of loose, incomplete-double to peony form with abundant petaloids, opening late in the camellia season on an open, vigorous, rapidly growing shrub with dark green foliage. It originated as a seedling raised by J.P. Illges of Columbus, Georgia, first flowering in 1951 and registered with the American Camellia Society in 1954; it went on to receive a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit. A white-marbled sport, Pink Champagne Variegated, is also grown. Plant in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, sheltered from hot afternoon sun.

common_name: Extravaganza Camellia (White-and-Pink Streaked Anemone-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; forms an upright, fairly large shrub over time, so give it a full season to root in before its first summer.

directions: Extravaganza lives up to its name with large anemone-form flowers in white to palest pink, irregularly streaked and splashed with deep pinkish red so that no two blooms match, opening midseason on an upright, compact-to-rounded evergreen shrub. The glossy dark green leaves have finely serrated edges typical of Camellia japonica. Its striking, unpredictable petal streaking makes it a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded border or woodland-edge planting. Grow in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil, and mulch to protect the shallow root system.

common_name: Lady Kay Camellia (Rose-Red and White Blotched Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; blooms mid-to-late spring, so fall planting establishes the root system well ahead of bloom.

directions: Lady Kay bears large, semi-double flowers in rose-red to pink marked with irregular white blotches, opening mid-to-late spring on a dense, evergreen shrub with dark green foliage. It arose in the United States around 1950 as a seedling of the historic French heirloom cultivar Ville de Nantes, inheriting a similarly bold, variable bicolor pattern. The late bloom season helps its flowers escape early-spring frost damage in cooler parts of its hardiness range. Grow in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil for the best flower color and form.

common_name: Sea Foam Camellia (Pure White Double Rose-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; a late-season bloomer, so fall planting lets it root in well before its late-winter-to-spring flower display.

directions: Sea Foam produces an abundance of medium-to-large, fully double, rose-form flowers in pure white with elegantly cupped petals, blooming late in the season from late winter through spring, a timing that helps the flowers avoid late-season freeze damage. It was introduced in 1959 by John Wiesner of Fernandina Beach, Florida, and forms a large, vigorous evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves. Its size and heavy late bloom make it well suited to a shaded specimen planting or informal screen. Grow in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; very slow-growing, so fall planting maximizes root establishment time before summer heat.

directions: Tanya is a dwarf, very slow-growing sasanqua with small, dark, glossy elliptical leaves and masses of small, lightly scented, deep pink, drooping flowers from mid to late autumn. Its low, spreading habit makes it useful as a groundcover, front-of-border edging plant, or container specimen where full-size sasanquas would be too large. As with other sasanquas, Tanya tolerates more sun than Camellia japonica but still performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates. Grow in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and keep evenly moist while establishing.
